intro:
In three sittings, you build one working program: a quote service, a program that gives a price for a job before anyone books it. A customer asks what it costs to send a parcel to Lisbon. The service asks three invented courier companies, Northline, Eastgate and Fjord, at the same time, and within 300 ms it answers with the cheapest price, or with the last good price marked stale. It runs on Netty 4.2 with Kotlin coroutines inside. When a customer hangs up, the calls to the couriers stop. When a crowd arrives, each courier gets only its share of calls, only harmless questions are asked twice, the slow courier gets a second call, customers the service can't serve in time hear "busy" at once, and the service closes at night in order. The tests prove each of those by counting calls, permits, cancellations and virtual milliseconds, never by timing.

The capstone draws on all of Part 2, and calls back its pictures as it goes. Lesson 1 is the post office of the Servers track: a clerk who owns a row of boxes and must never stop to make a phone call, the in-tray, and the full out-tray with two painted marks. Lesson 2 is the home cook of the Kotlin coroutines track: texting three shops at once, the kitchen timer, a course that goes out only when all its dishes are ready, the guests calling dinner off, and the neighbour's ticket at the fence. Lesson 3 adds the bakery's slip "send me 10 more" from the Reactive track, the shelf in the hatch from Kotlin Flow in depth, and from Part 1 the grill tokens, Little's law and closing time. There is little new theory. Each section shows what breaks if you choose differently, then names the earlier lesson that explains why.

The lab is `labs/quotes`, one package per lesson (`workbench.quotes.l01` to `l03`). Each lesson's starting code contains the previous lesson's solution, so you can start any sitting fresh. Lesson 1's lab is in Java; lessons 2 and 3 are in Kotlin, with lesson 1's Java server carried along. From `labs/`, run `./gradlew :quotes:test --tests 'workbench.quotes.lNN.*'` until it passes; `./gradlew :quotes:solutionTest` runs the same tests against the reference answers. Servers bind `127.0.0.1` on a free port, coroutine tests run on virtual time, and the Try-it demos run with `./gradlew :quotes:demo -Pmain=...`, in Kotlin and in Java. Install JDK 25; the labs compile with release 21.
cheatsheet:
## The service in one picture

A customer sends `7 LISBON`: request 7, a parcel to Lisbon. Within 300 ms the server answers `7 OK LISBON 12.42 northline` (the cheapest price that arrived in time, and who offered it), `7 STALE LISBON 12.41 eastgate` (no courier answered, so the last live price, labelled as old), `7 ERR busy` (the service is full) or `7 ERR no quote for LISBON`. Replies can overtake each other, so the client matches them by the id.

## The pictures behind the design

| Picture from Part 2 (and Part 1) | Where it came from | What it became in the service |
|---|---|---|
| the clerk who owns a row of boxes and never makes a phone call | Netty: the event loop and the channel pipeline | one event loop per set of channels; `QuoteSource.quote` returns a future at once |
| the clerk's in-tray | the same lesson | `whenCompleteAsync(..., ctx.executor())`: the reply is written on the channel's own loop |
| the page count on the envelope | Netty in practice: codecs, flow control and leaks | `LineBasedFrameDecoder(64)`: a frame limit, then a close |
| the full out-tray with two painted marks | the same lesson | the water marks (32 KiB and 64 KiB) and `isWritable()` |
| the packer's slip, "send me 10 more" | Why reactive: push, pull and backpressure | auto-read: read a client only while its replies can leave and fewer than 16 requests wait |
| the neighbour's ticket at the fence | Coroutines meet Java: futures, Reactor, virtual threads | `scope.future { }`: a `CompletableFuture` tied to the request's coroutine |
| texting three shops at once | Builders: launch, async, runBlocking, coroutineScope | `async` for each courier, then await: the slowest decides, not the sum |
| a course goes out only when all its dishes are ready | Structured concurrency: scopes, jobs and the tree | `coroutineScope`: right when every answer is needed, wrong for a price |
| one burnt tray doesn't spoil the bake sale | Exceptions: launch vs async, SupervisorJob, handlers | `supervisorScope`, and `SupervisorJob()` in the service's scope |
| the kitchen timer; the guests calling dinner off | Cancellation and timeouts | `withTimeoutOrNull` per call; a hang-up cancels the coroutine and every courier call |
| the rehearsal dinner on a fake clock | Shared state and testing coroutines | `runTest` and an injected `StandardTestDispatcher` |
| the 20 grill tokens | Using virtual threads: one per task, limits with semaphores | a `Semaphore` bulkhead for each courier |
| the broken oven, baked again | Errors, retries and timeouts | retries with backoff and jitter, for idempotent couriers only |
| the shelf in the hatch: wait, or bin a dumpling | Buffering: buffer, conflate, collectLatest and fusion | admission with `tryAcquire`: full means `ERR busy` at once, never a queue |
| closing the kitchen at night | Pools in production: names, errors, context, shutdown | stop accepting, stop admitting, drain, `cancelAndJoin`, close |
| fewer clerks, or cheaper clerks | Blocking IO, threads and the C10K problem | the design review: event loop, or one virtual thread per connection |

## The shell (lesson 1)

| Guard | Why | How | Picture it |
|---|---|---|---|
| a frame limit | a client that never sends a newline can't make the server keep its bytes forever | `LineBasedFrameDecoder(64)`; a longer line gets `ERR line too long`, then a close | the page count on the envelope |
| a request id | replies leave when prices arrive, so they overtake each other | `7 LISBON` gets `7 OK LISBON 12.42 northline` | a ticket stub matched to its coat |
| never block the loop | one wait stalls every channel on that loop | `quote` returns a future; no `join()`, `get()` or `runBlocking` in a handler | the clerk never makes the phone call |
| finish on the loop | the handler's state stays on one thread, so no locks | `whenCompleteAsync(callback, ctx.executor())` | the note goes into the clerk's in-tray |
| backpressure | writes never block; unread replies and pending futures pile up in your memory | auto-read only while writable and fewer than 16 requests wait, plus `FlowControlHandler` | the slip "send me 10 more", and the out-tray's two painted marks |
| close on purpose | a close right after `flush()` can drop bytes; nobody reads a hung-up client's answers | close from the write's future; cancel the futures in flight in `channelInactive` | |
| an ordered server close | no new work while you stop | stop accepting, close the `ChannelGroup`, then `shutdownGracefully` | closing time |

```java
// the handler never waits: hand the future back, finish on this channel's loop
CompletableFuture<Quote> quote = source.quote(r.destination());
inFlight.add(quote);
updateReading(ctx);                                      // autoRead = writable && inFlight < 16
quote.whenCompleteAsync((q, e) -> {
    inFlight.remove(quote);
    if (ctx.channel().isActive()) ctx.writeAndFlush(e == null ? ok(r.id(), q) : error(r.id(), e));
    updateReading(ctx);
}, ctx.executor());
```

```kotlin
// the handler never waits: hand the future back, finish on this channel's loop
val quote = source.quote(r.destination)
inFlight += quote
updateReading(ctx)                                       // isAutoRead = isWritable && inFlight.size < 16
quote.whenCompleteAsync({ q, e ->
    inFlight -= quote
    if (ctx.channel().isActive) ctx.writeAndFlush(if (e == null) ok(r.id, q) else error(r.id, e))
    updateReading(ctx)
}, ctx.executor())
```

## The fan-out (lesson 2)

| Decision | Choice | What breaks otherwise | Picture it |
|---|---|---|---|
| start | `async` for each courier, then await | one after another takes the sum, 620 ms instead of 300 | text three shops at once |
| scope | `supervisorScope` | `coroutineScope` cancels the other couriers at the first failure | one burnt tray doesn't spoil the bake sale |
| deadline | `withTimeoutOrNull(deadline)` around each call | one timeout around the fan-out throws away answers that arrived | the kitchen timer |
| failures | await each call in a try; failed or late is `null` | one bad courier fails every request | |
| cancels | rethrow only after `currentCoroutineContext().ensureActive()` says it was yours | a courier's own timeout ends the request | the message that dinner is off, only when it's for you |
| nobody answered | the last live price, marked `STALE`, else `NoQuoteException` | a stale answer refreshing the cache serves an old price forever | |
| the Java edge | `scope.future { }` in a scope with `SupervisorJob()` | `supplyAsync` futures don't stop the work; a plain `Job` lets one failure cancel every request | the neighbour's ticket, tied to the pot |

```kotlin
suspend fun quote(destination: String): Quote {
    val answers = supervisorScope {                                  // a failed call fails alone
        providers.map { p -> async { withTimeoutOrNull(deadline) { p.quote(destination) } } }
            .map { d ->
                try { d.await() }
                catch (e: CancellationException) { currentCoroutineContext().ensureActive(); null }
                catch (e: Exception) { null }
            }
    }.filterNotNull()
    val best = answers.minByOrNull { it.price } ?: return cache.lastGood(destination)?.asStale()
        ?: throw NoQuoteException(destination)
    return best.also { cache.remember(it) }
}
```

```java
// Reactor: every outcome becomes a value at its source, then Mono.zip
Mono<Optional<Quote>> inTime(Mono<Quote> call) {
    return call.timeout(DEADLINE).map(Optional::of)
            .onErrorResume(e -> Mono.just(Optional.empty()))
            .defaultIfEmpty(Optional.empty());               // or an empty source empties the zip
}
```

## Under load (lesson 3)

| Guard | Rule | Picture it |
|---|---|---|
| bulkhead | a `Semaphore` per courier, sized from its contract; a permit around every single call, hedges included | the grill tokens |
| retry | idempotent couriers only, `IOException` only, waits jittered by 0.5 to 1.5, inside the deadline | the oven baked again, but not by every packer in the same second |
| hedge | idempotent couriers with a slow tail only, after about p95, with its own permit; cancel the loser | text a second branch of the same shop |
| admission | `tryAcquire()` at the door; full means `ERR busy` at once, never a queue | the full shelf: a loud bin, not a waiting cook |
| shutdown | stop accepting, stop admitting, drain within a grace period, `cancelAndJoin()` the rest, close connections and loops | closing time at the post office |

```kotlin
override suspend fun quote(destination: String): Quote {
    val once: suspend () -> Quote = { permits.withPermit { delegate.quote(destination) } }   // every call
    if (!delegate.idempotent) return once()                                                  // a booking: once
    val attempt: suspend () -> Quote = if (hedgeAfter == null) once else ({ hedged(hedgeAfter, once) })
    return retrying(backoff, random, attempt)                                                // jittered
}
```

```java
// Java on virtual threads: the same rules with blocking calls
Quote quote(String destination) throws IOException, InterruptedException {
    if (!delegate.idempotent()) return once(destination);  // a booking: once
    for (int n = 1; ; n++) {
        try { return once(destination); }                  // once() = acquire, call, release
        catch (IOException e) {
            if (n > backoff.retries()) throw e;
            Thread.sleep(jittered(backoff.nominal(n)));
        }
    }
}
```

## Numbers from this track's demos

| What | Measured |
|---|---|
| 10 clients, one loop, a 100 ms courier | `join()`: 1,163 ms, one price at a time; future handed back: 146 ms, ten at once (one run on a busy machine) |
| 20,000 pipelined requests, client not reading | no policy: about 2 MB of replies queued (it varies); auto-read rule: 716,915 bytes; plus `FlowControlHandler`: 67,584 |
| fan-out of 120, 300 and 200 ms | 620 ms in turn, 300 ms with `async`, 250 ms with a 250 ms deadline |
| 1,000 customers retrying together | no jitter: all in one millisecond; jitter 0.5: at most 18 in any millisecond |
| hedge after 80 ms, every 20th call slow | p99 600 ms down to 120 ms, 210 calls instead of 200 |
| 500 requests, 10 permits x 50 ms, 300 ms deadline | queued: 50 live, 450 slow failures; admit 50: 50 live, 450 `ERR busy` at once |

## Little's law for every limit

In flight = arrival rate x time. A courier that allows 10 calls at once and answers in 50 ms serves at most 200 calls a second; inside a 300 ms deadline, that is about 60 requests. Bulkhead permits come from the contract, admission comes from what the couriers can answer before the deadline, and every retry and hedge counts as a call.

## Event loop or virtual threads

Picture it: the post office's two ways out of the crowd, fewer clerks who never wait, or a cheap clerk for every customer.

| Pick | When |
|---|---|
| event loop and coroutines (this design) | the service lives on Netty, Vert.x or Quarkus; connections in the hundreds of thousands; you need auto-read, decoders and flow control; the courier clients are non-blocking and a cancel must reach them |
| one virtual thread per connection | the courier clients only block (JDBC and the like); connections in the thousands; the team prefers plain Java |
| either way | bulkheads, deadlines, admission and an ordered shutdown stay. Virtual threads remove the pool, and with it the one limit nobody wrote down |

## Test recipes

- Count, don't time: hold prices open with a fake you control, then count calls, probe tasks, permits and cancellations. A 5-second wait only bounds how long a failure takes.
- Coroutines on virtual time: `runTest`, and pass `StandardTestDispatcher(testScheduler)` to the class that owns a scope. `currentTime` is exact; a `delay` on `Dispatchers.Default` is real.
- Pipelines without sockets: `EmbeddedChannel(handlers)`, `writeInbound`, then `runPendingTasks()` before `readOutbound()` when replies are written from tasks.
- Real servers: bind `127.0.0.1` on port 0, read with a socket timeout, assert with latches, and always close the server in `finally`.
recap: The program is a quote service for parcel prices: a Netty shell, a coroutine fan-out to three couriers under a 300 ms deadline, and the guards that keep it standing under load.

The event loop never waits, like the clerk who never makes the phone call. Handlers hand futures back and finish in `whenCompleteAsync(..., ctx.executor())`, and a test proves the loop is free by counting calls and probe tasks.
Auto-read is the only tap, the packer's slip at the network's level: read while writable and under 16 in flight, with `FlowControlHandler` holding lines already decoded.
A best-of fan-out uses `supervisorScope` and `withTimeoutOrNull` per call, and rethrows only its own cancel. With no answer, it serves a stale price, labelled as such, or fails clearly.
`scope.future { }` in a `SupervisorJob` scope gives Java a future whose cancel reaches every courier call, so a hang-up stops the work.
Each courier gets a bulkhead sized by Little's law. Only idempotent calls are retried, with jitter, and only the slow, idempotent courier is hedged.
Turn work away at the door with `tryAcquire` and a clear `ERR busy`, and shut down in order: stop accepting, stop admitting, drain, `cancelAndJoin`, close.
Event loop or virtual threads, the limits stay. Pick the model by where the waiting happens and by what the courier clients can do.

quiz.q: Which line in a Netty handler blocks the event loop?
options: `quote.whenCompleteAsync(callback, ctx.executor())`
`ctx.writeAndFlush(reply)` called from a courier's thread
`source.quote(destination).join()`
`ctx.channel().config().setAutoRead(false)`
quiz.why: `join()` holds the loop thread until the price arrives, so every channel on that loop waits. The callback runs later as a task, a write from another thread is queued onto the loop, and changing auto-read returns at once.

quiz.q: The handler turns auto-read off after 16 requests, yet it still receives 2,000 more requests from the bytes of one socket read. What is missing?
options: A bigger high water mark
A `FlowControlHandler` between the decoders and the handler
A call to `ctx.read()` in `channelRead0`
`TCP_NODELAY` on the channel
quiz.why: Auto-read stops the next socket read, not the lines the frame decoder already holds. `FlowControlHandler` keeps those decoded messages while auto-read is off and releases them as reading resumes. `ctx.read()` would do the opposite: ask for more.

quiz.q: Why does this track's test for a free event loop count calls and probe tasks instead of checking that a probe runs within 300 ms?
options: On a busy build machine a healthy loop can miss a time limit, while a blocked loop's counts are wrong at any speed
Netty doesn't let you time tasks on an event loop
Counting is faster to run
Virtual time doesn't work for Netty, so nothing can be timed
quiz.why: Timings depend on the machine's load; counts depend only on what the code did. A loop stuck in `join()` makes 1 call however fast the machine is, and the test's 5-second wait only bounds how long the failure takes to report.

quiz.q: A price needs any one of three couriers' answers. Which scope runs the three calls?
options: `coroutineScope`, so a failure cancels the rest
`GlobalScope`, so the calls outlive a cancelled request
`runBlocking`, so the event loop waits for the answers
`supervisorScope`, so each call fails alone
quiz.why: With `supervisorScope`, a failed child keeps its exception for `await`, and the other calls carry on. `coroutineScope` is right when every answer is needed. `GlobalScope` leaks the calls, and `runBlocking` blocks the loop.

quiz.q: Each call is `async { withTimeout(300) { c.quote(d) } }` in a supervisor fan-out, and the await rethrows every `CancellationException`. A courier is slow. What happens?
options: The slow courier counts as no answer
The request ends with `TimeoutCancellationException`, as if it had been cancelled
The request waits for the slow courier
The other couriers are cancelled, but the request succeeds
quiz.why: `withTimeout` signals with `TimeoutCancellationException`, a `CancellationException`, and the catch passes it up as if the whole request were cancelled. Use `withTimeoutOrNull`, and check `ensureActive()` before rethrowing a cancel.

quiz.q: Lesson 1's Java handler cancels the future when the client hangs up. Which way of writing `QuoteSource.quote` turns that cancel into cancelled courier calls?
options: `CompletableFuture.supplyAsync(() -> blockingBest(destination), pool)`
`CompletableFuture.completedFuture(runBlocking { best.quote(destination) })`
`scope.future { best.quote(destination) }` in a scope the service owns
`GlobalScope.async { best.quote(destination) }.asCompletableFuture()` with no scope to close
quiz.why: The `future` builder links both ways: cancelling the future cancels the coroutine, and the cancel travels down to the courier calls. `supplyAsync`'s cancel stops nothing, `runBlocking` blocks the event loop before returning, and `GlobalScope` work has no owner to close it at shutdown.

options: Northline: it only looks up a price, so a repeat is harmless, and it has a slow tail worth cutting
Fjord: its prices are bookings that hold a place on a van, and it is the slowest
Every courier, after the same 80 ms
None: hedging always doubles the load
quiz.why: A hedge is a duplicate request, so only an idempotent courier qualifies, and it pays off only where the tail hurts. Hedging after about p95 costs about 5% more calls, not double. A booking is never repeated.

quiz.q: Where does a courier's bulkhead permit belong?
options: Around the whole retry loop, so a request holds one permit for all its attempts
Around each single call, so a pause before a retry holds nothing and a hedge needs its own permit
Around the whole fan-out, one permit per request
Nowhere: the deadline already limits the calls
quiz.why: The permit limits calls in flight to the courier, so it wraps exactly one call. Around the retry loop, it would be held through the pauses; around the fan-out, it would count requests instead of calls; and a deadline limits time, not how many calls run at once.

quiz.q: A burst of 500 requests meets a courier that can answer about 60 within the deadline. What does admission with `tryAcquire` change?
options: It gets live answers to all 500, just later
It cuts the live answers to almost none
It makes the courier faster
The same number of live answers, but the rest hear `ERR busy` at once instead of failing after the deadline
quiz.why: Requests beyond what the courier can serve in time fail either way. Shedding makes them fail in a millisecond, early enough to try another copy of the service, and nothing waits in a queue or on the event loop. In the demo, 50 requests got live answers in both runs.

quiz.q: When should this service stay on an event loop instead of moving to one virtual thread per connection?
options: When the courier clients only block
When the team prefers plain Java and connections number in the thousands
When it already runs on Netty or Vert.x, connections number in the hundreds of thousands, or the courier clients are non-blocking and a cancel must reach them
Always: event loops are faster per request
quiz.why: The event loop pays off for huge numbers of connections, control over the protocol and non-blocking clients. Blocking clients and plain Java favour virtual threads. Neither model makes a single request faster, and both still need the bulkheads, deadlines and admission.
